title: Sesshin
hook: days of intensive silent sitting in a Zen monastery or center

segments.voice: This week the herdsman rode home, forgot the ox, forgot himself in an empty circle, and walked into the market. Yesterday: two schools, koans and just sitting. What did you name that each one offers? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two, and the week closes.

Before dawn, a wooden clapper sounds down a dark hallway. People roll up their bedding without a word and file into the meditation hall. Shoes in a row by the door. Cushions in a row along the wall. Nobody chats over breakfast, because breakfast is eaten in silence too, and so is lunch, and so is the walk back to the hall. This goes on, not for an hour, but for days. In Zen monasteries and in Zen centers in ordinary towns, this stretch of time has a name. Today's word: sesshin.
screen: `A CLAPPER BEFORE DAWN.` → `SILENCE AT EVERY MEAL.` → `NOT AN HOUR. DAYS.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Sesshin is Japanese, often rendered as gathering the mind, or touching the mind. Picture water spread thin across a table, then drawn together into one bowl. That's the image: attention that is usually scattered across every small thing in a day, collected in one place. Second, the shape of a day. Sesshin is mostly zazen, sitting, in periods marked by a bell. Between them comes slow walking. There are chants, meals, a period of work, and a talk from the teacher. Tradition fills the gaps with forms: when to bow, where to put your bowl, how to enter the hall. The forms aren't there to make it hard. They're there so nobody has to decide anything. When there's nothing to plan, the mind has fewer places to run. Third, the silence. Participants don't talk, and some keep their eyes lowered. Some who have sat sesshin describe the first day or two as the loudest part: the silence outside lets every thought inside be heard. Teachers in both schools you met yesterday hold sesshin. A Rinzai sesshin may lean on koan work and meetings with the teacher; a Soto sesshin may lean on just sitting. Each is still sesshin. Fourth, why anyone would do this. An evening sit is a single drop of water on a stone. Days of sitting, one after another, give the mind time to settle in a way one short sit rarely can. And then it ends. People bow, speak their first words, and go home to traffic and email. What they bring back is not the silence itself, but some memory of what a gathered mind is like.
screen: `GATHERING THE SCATTERED MIND.` · `SITTING, WALKING, EATING, WORKING.` · `FORMS SO NO ONE HAS TO DECIDE.` · `DAYS LET SOMETHING SETTLE.` · then, large: `SESSHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit comfortably and close your eyes, or rest them on the floor. Picture one day of sesshin, as if you were there. The clapper before dawn. Your cushion in its row. The first bell. Breathing in silence beside people whose names you may not know. Then let the picture go, and notice: right now, in this small sit, you're doing the same thing they do. When the mind scatters, gather it back to one breath. The bell holds the time.
Sesshin. Days of silent, intensive practice in a Zen monastery or center: sitting, walking, eating and working, with the mind gathered in one place. Today's word.

Your line: gathering the mind. Today, choose one ordinary task, washing a cup or walking to the car, and do it the way a sesshin would: only that, without talking. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Zen monasteries and many Zen centers hold sesshin, retreats of several days in which participants keep silence and follow a fixed schedule of sitting, walking meditation, chanting, work, meals and talks from the teacher.

myth: sesshin is a single long sitting with no breaks
the days mix sitting with walking, chanting, meals, work and a teacher's talk.
both Rinzai and Soto teachers hold sesshin
the emphasis may differ, koans in one, just sitting in the other, but each holds sesshin.
the silence is kept even at meals
meals are eaten in silence too.

fork.setup: it's the first full day of sesshin. the hall is silent, but your mind is louder than it has been in months. what does this mean?
options: you're doing it wrong and should leave.
it's common: outer silence lets inner noise be heard.
you should start talking to quiet it.
fork.reveal: some who sit sesshin describe the first day or two as the loudest. the days that follow give it time to settle.

original.note: Japanese: sesshin, rendered 'gathering' or 'touching' the mind. some communities write it 摂心.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quiet weekend away.
what it means: days of silent sitting, walking, eating and working, all held in one schedule.
what a scholar hears: two spellings, 接心 and 摂心, both read sesshin, often glossed as touching the mind and gathering the mind.

sources.work: Zen communal practice, Rinzai and Soto
